Chapter 37

Explore, and diagnostics

A dynamic page reading prerendered data, debounced with runed, grouped with Intl.DisplayNames, linking with typed resolve(); and a page that reads the server’s own OpenTelemetry spans out of a ring buffer through src/instrumentation.server.ts.

By the end of this chapter

Mix prerendered data into a per-request page, use a utility library where it earns its place, and turn SvelteKit 3’s built-in tracing into a page you can read.

Three things worth stopping on, and one small one. await places() at the top of the script — allowed in async mode — is the prerendered gazetteer: the page is dynamic because its header knows who you are, and its data is static, and that split is what prerender remote functions are for. (On the server, rendering this page, the same call fetches that file from the app’s public address, and falls back to running the function when it cannot — chapter 17 says why the function is dynamic for that day.) Intl.DisplayNames turns country codes into names in the page’s language, a hundred strings per locale nobody translated. And runed’s Debounced follows query with a delay: settled.current changes 150 ms after the last keystroke, so the list is not rebuilt on every one. It takes a getter, so query stays a plain $state. The coordinates under each place read as a place — 38.72° N, 9.14° W — and the compass letters are messages, because they are words: east is O in German and L in Portuguese, and west is O in Portuguese. The small one is clear(). Both “clear” buttons remove themselves — the one in the field shows only while there is a query, the one in the empty state only while nothing matches — and a button that disappears under the keyboard’s focus drops focus to the top of the document, so a keyboard user who cleared the search had to tab back through the header to type again. clear() empties the query and puts focus in the field, through a bind:this, which is where the next thing typed belongs. And query does not quite start empty. On a page the server rendered, the field is there and usable before the JavaScript is, and what a person types into it in that second was wiped when the page hydrated — bind:value writes the state into the input, and the state was the empty string the server knew. The script runs while the server’s input is still on the page, so the state starts from whatever is in it: the same cure as keepTyped() for the sign-in form in chapter 34, for a plain input. On a client-side navigation there is no server input to read, and it starts empty after all.

Two href() calls, one with a parameter and one without, and resolve() with the route id underneath each. The route id for the new-trip page is /(site)/(app)/trips/new?place=… — route ids include their groups, which surprises people the first time, and since SvelteKit 2.54, so in every 3.x, they may carry their search string — and resolve gives back /trips/new?place=lisbon, type-checked against the routes that exist, before the language prefix goes on. It gives that back on the server as well as in the browser because paths.relative is false; with the default, the server’s answer was ./trips/new?place=lisbon, and chapter 25 tells what became of it. The place links to its guide when one exists, through guideForPlace from chapter 36. The countries are a grid in reading order — one column on a phone, two from 48em, three from 64em, align-items: start so a short country does not stretch to its neighbour’s height — and each country is unbroken, its places one under another. They were CSS columns once, columns: 3 18rem, and columns fill *down* first: the alphabet ran down a 4,000px page and started again at the top of the next column, so “Hong Kong” sat beside “Argentina” and a person scanning across for “Japan” never found it. A grid of *places* had been wrong the other way, leaving each country a row of one or two cards and the rest of the width empty; a grid of countries is the shape the content has. A place is a card and not a link — its two buttons are the links — so it does not lift on hover, because a lift says “this is a link”. The search row sticks under the header and draws its hairline once it is stuck, which a zero-height sentinel and an IntersectionObserver attached to it decide; the browser’s blue clear button is replaced by a ghost one of ours, and on a phone the count is the places alone, so the row stays one row.

Why runed, for one debounce

A debounce is fifteen lines to write and one to import, and the fifteen lines are the kind that get a subtle bug — a timer that survives unmount, a value that updates once too often. runed is a collection of such utilities written against runes by people who maintain Bits UI, and Debounced, useEventListener, ElementSize and PersistedState are the ones most apps reach for. The rule from chapter 01 holds: it sits behind one line, and removing it is writing the fifteen lines. Chapter 43 has the longer argument about utility libraries.

Diagnostics: the server’s own traces

With tracing.server on, SvelteKit emits an OpenTelemetry span for every handle, load, form action and remote function. src/instrumentation.server.ts is loaded before any application code — in development through Vite, in production because adapter-node wires it in front of the entry point — and registers a tracer provider with one processor that hands every finished span to an exporter. The usual exporter sends spans to a collector over the network; this one keeps the last three hundred in memory, which is all a single-process app needs to answer “what did that request do?” on its own page.

The ring is module-level state shared by every request, which is usually the bug and here is the point: it holds nothing private, and only the diagnostics page reads it. record flattens a span to the fields the page shows; recentSpans returns a copy, newest first, so a reader cannot reach into the ring. The exporter is the OpenTelemetry interface — an export with a callback, and a shutdown — implemented in twelve lines.

The page is one query and a table: version, Node version, uptime formatted by Intl units; the live rooms with their watcher counts, from chapter 19; and the spans, indented when they have a parent. Refresh calls diagnostics().refresh(), and the table redraws because the report is {const report = $derived(await diagnostics())}. A failed report is printed by the failed snippet through boundaryMessage, like every boundary in the app (chapter 27), and a child span’s indent and a failed span’s coral chip are class={…} objects (chapter 25). It was a bare {const} at first, which awaits the first report and keeps it: the button fetched a new one and the page went on showing the old, until an end-to-end test pressed it (chapter 46). Open the trip page in another tab, come back, refresh — and the watchTrip span is there, with the heartbeat commands under it, which is how the presence loop in chapter 26 was first seen as a column of identical rows.

Checkpoint

  • You can say why the explore page is dynamic and its data is prerendered, and what each half costs.
  • You can give the route id for the new-trip page and say why it looks like that.
  • You can trace a span from tracing: { server: true } through the instrumentation file to the table.
